questions.title: R8.1 · Cost unit
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe a cost unit.
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: What precisely are you costing?
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A cost unit is the item/activity whose cost is measured, such as one product, a job, a batch, a patient-day or a service consultation. Define it before classifying direct and indirect costs.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R8.2 · Uses of full cost
questions.promptMarkdown: For which decisions is full cost information relevant?
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: Separate long-run recovery from a one-off spare-capacity order.
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Full cost can support longer-run pricing/cost recovery, product/job profitability and inventory/work-in-progress measurement under the course approach. An allocated full cost is not automatically the relevant cost for a short-run incremental decision.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R8.3 · Two cost classifications
questions.promptMarkdown: Differentiate direct/indirect costs from variable/fixed costs.
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: Traceability and behaviour answer different questions.
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Direct costs can be economically traced to a specified cost unit; indirect costs are shared and require allocation. Variable/fixed describes how total cost changes with activity. A cost can be direct and fixed, or indirect and variable.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R8.4 · Four combinations
questions.promptMarkdown: Give two examples each of direct variable, direct fixed, indirect variable and indirect fixed costs.
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: State your cost object; classification can change with it.
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: For a product line: direct variable = raw material and piece-rate assembly; direct fixed = dedicated machine lease and a product-specific design licence; indirect variable = shared machine power and pooled consumables varying with output; indirect fixed = factory rent and the general factory manager salary. State assumptions that make tracing uneconomic for the indirect examples.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R8.5 · Indirect cost problem
questions.promptMarkdown: What is the general problem with indirect costs in decision making?
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: Allocation bases can change reported product profitability.
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Indirect costs cannot be traced directly to the unit, so allocation needs an assumption or driver. An arbitrary basis can distort product/job costs and pricing. Allocating an existing fixed cost does not show that accepting a job causes that cost.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R8.6 · Traditional versus ABC
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe and differentiate traditional full costing and activity-based costing.
rubricChecks: Classified costing systems, direct/indirect items, or activity drivers accurately for the stated business context
Explained both the decision usefulness and practical limitations (cost-benefit, market demand, arbitrary pools) of full/ABC costs
hints: Compare one/few broad volume drivers with activity pools.
Compare single volume-based absorption rates (DLH/MH) against multi-pool ABC cost drivers, weighing improved accuracy against measurement cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Traditional absorption costing allocates overhead using a blanket or departmental rate such as labour or machine hours. ABC groups overhead by activities and assigns it using drivers such as setups, inspections or orders. Both allocate indirect costs; ABC is more detailed, still relies on assumptions and costs more to maintain.
questions.pitfall: Saying ABC changes direct cost tracing (direct costs are traced identically; ABC only refines indirect overhead pools).

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R10.1 · ARR · pros and cons
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe the pros and cons of the **Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)** method of investment appraisal *(Reading Assignment Chapter 10, Q1a)*.
rubricChecks: Stated key pros: simple percentage measure familiar to managers and aligned with ROCE performance evaluation
Stated core cons: uses accounting profit rather than cash flows and completely ignores the time value of money
Noted additional cons: ignores project scale/duration and allows competing definitions (initial vs average investment)
hints: Compare the intuitive appeal of a percentage return based on familiar accrual profit/ROCE against cash-flow and time-value principles.

List at least two advantages (familiarity to managers, links with external ROCE reporting) and three drawbacks (uses accounting profit not cash, ignores time value of money, ignores project scale/life, sensitive to depreciation/average-investment definitions).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Pros of ARR:**
- Expressed as a percentage return that managers and investors readily understand and compare with **ROCE**.
- Evaluates profitability across the entire life of the project (unlike ordinary payback).

**Cons of ARR:**
- Uses **accounting profit** (affected by depreciation/accrual conventions) rather than cash flows.
- **Ignores the time value of money** — £1 of profit in Year 5 counts the same as £1 in Year 1.
- **Ignores project scale** (a tiny project with 40% ARR may add far less wealth than a large project with 25% ARR) and has competing formula variants.
questions.pitfall: Treating ARR as a discounted cash-flow return comparable to the cost of capital.

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R10.2 · Payback period · pros and cons
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe the pros and cons of the **Payback Period (PP)** method of investment appraisal *(Reading Assignment Chapter 10, Q1b)*.
rubricChecks: Stated key pros: quick, intuitive cash-based measure highlighting liquidity and early capital recovery under high uncertainty
Stated fatal cons: ignores all cash flows occurring after the payback date and ignores the time value of money (unless discounted payback is used)
Noted that payback lacks an objective wealth-maximising cut-off target
hints: Think about liquidity, risk of obsolescence, and simplicity versus wealth maximisation.

Highlight why payback is a useful quick risk/liquidity screen, then state its two fatal theoretical flaws: ignoring the time value of money within payback and ignoring ALL cash flows after the payback cut-off.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Pros of Payback Period:**
- Uses **cash flows** rather than accounting profits and is quick and intuitive to compute.
- Emphasises **liquidity** and rapid recovery, acting as a rough screen when technology/demand risk makes distant forecasts unreliable.

**Cons of Payback Period:**
- **Ignores all cash flows after the payback point**, biasing against strategic projects whose main payoffs arrive later.
- **Ignores the time value of money** within the payback window (two projects both paying back in Year 3 can have very different Year 1 vs Year 3 timing).
- Not directly anchored to **owners' wealth maximisation**; the maximum acceptable payback period is arbitrary.
questions.pitfall: Saying discounted payback cures all flaws of payback — it still ignores every cash flow after the recovery date!

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: R10.3 · Net present value · pros and cons
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe the pros and cons of the **Net Present Value (NPV)** method of investment appraisal *(Reading Assignment Chapter 10, Q1c)*.
rubricChecks: Stated theoretical gold-standard pros: uses all relevant cash flows, discounts for time value and risk, and directly measures £ change in owners' wealth
Noted that NPV handles mutually exclusive projects of different scales and non-conventional cash flows cleanly
Stated practical cons: requires estimating an appropriate cost of capital and communicating an absolute £ value rather than an intuitive % margin
hints: Evaluate NPV against the three requirements of a theoretically sound investment rule: all cash flows, time value/risk, and direct £ change in shareholder wealth.
For cons, focus on practical implementation challenges: estimating the cost of capital, forecasting multi-year incremental cash flows, and explaining an absolute £ figure to non-financial managers.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Pros of NPV (Theoretical Gold Standard):**
- Incorporates **all relevant cash flows** over the entire project life.
- Accounts fully for the **time value of money** and project **risk** via the opportunity cost of capital.
- Directly measures the **net £ increase in owners' wealth** (additive across projects and reliable when ranking mutually exclusive projects of different sizes).

**Cons of NPV:**
- Requires estimating the **cost of capital** upfront.
- Non-specialist managers sometimes find an absolute £ value harder to interpret as a 'margin of safety' than a percentage rate.
questions.pitfall: Claiming NPV has theoretical ranking defects — its limitations are practical estimation inputs (cash forecasts and discount rate), not the decision rule itself.

questions.title: R10.4 · Internal rate of return · pros and cons
questions.promptMarkdown: Describe the pros and cons of the **Internal Rate of Return (IRR)** method of investment appraisal *(Reading Assignment Chapter 10, Q1d)*.
rubricChecks: Stated key pros: considers all cash flows and time value of money while expressing return as an intuitive % yield
Stated scale flaw: ignores investment size, so ranking mutually exclusive projects by IRR % can destroy shareholder wealth
Stated non-conventional cash-flow flaw: sign reversals (e.g. decommissioning outlays) can produce multiple IRRs or no real IRR
hints: Start with why managers love IRR (time-adjusted cash-flow percentage yield compared against a hurdle rate).
Then list IRR's three classic traps vs NPV: ignoring project scale on mutually exclusive choices, multiple/no IRRs when cash-flow signs flip more than once, and reinvestment/timing ranking conflicts.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Pros of IRR:**
- Uses **cash flows** across the project's full life and incorporates the **time value of money**.
- Expressed as a **percentage yield**, allowing managers to see headroom above the hurdle rate without needing an exact discount rate to start the calculation.

**Cons of IRR:**
- **Ignores project scale:** cannot reliably rank mutually exclusive projects of different sizes (higher % on small outlay vs lower % on large outlay).
- **Non-conventional cash flows** (more than one sign change) can yield **multiple IRRs** or no real IRR.
- Can conflict with NPV when cash-flow timing profiles differ across mutually exclusive projects.
questions.pitfall: Choosing a small project with a 35% IRR over a mutually exclusive large project with a 22% IRR that generates a much higher £ NPV.

pacing.rationale: Short conceptual reading/review prompt: 5 min to formulate definition + example while learning, 2.5 min for rapid exam recall.

questions.title: D1 · Explain the foundation.
questions.promptMarkdown: Name the two fundamental information qualities. Explain why maximizing sales or this year's accounting profit need not maximize owners' wealth. Distinguish financial from management accounting and explain why managers may use financial statements too.
rubricChecks: Matched specific stakeholder groups to concrete resource-allocation or risk decisions
Identified shared interest in liquidity, profitability, and long-term viability across internal and external users
hints: Compare relevance and faithful representation, then timing/risk of returns rather than sales alone.
Link each group's decision to specific solvency, profitability, or risk information, noting where internal managers and external investors look at the same metrics.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Relevance and faithful representation. Owners' wealth concerns the value created for owners, including timing and risk; sales can rise without sufficient margin, and accounting profit can rise while capital earns less than its opportunity cost. Financial accounting provides general-purpose reporting especially for external users; management accounting supports internal decisions with tailored information. Managers can also use financial statements. The wealth objective is the textbook's working assumption, not a claim that every organisation pursues only one goal.
questions.pitfall: Listing user groups without explaining the concrete decision each group uses accounting data to make.

pacing.rationale: Multi-part conceptual critique requiring separate evaluation of 3–6 accounting claims or classifications.

questions.title: D12 · Price reliable information.
questions.promptMarkdown: In the course's simple financing model, investment is 100, internal equity 20, high payoff 200, low payoff 120, and each type has probability 0.5. Investors break even in expectation. For an entrepreneur who knows the project is high type, calculate the outside ownership share with a credible report and without one, and the gross benefit of disclosure. Assume reporting does not change the investment requirement or payoff distribution. Explain why the benefit is not automatically a net gain.
rubricChecks: Calculated outside share with credible report = 40% vs without report = 50% (pooled value 160)
Calculated gross disclosure benefit to high-type owner = $(50\% - 40\%) \times 200 = 20$
Explained that audit/reporting costs must be $< 20$ for a strictly positive net gain
hints: Find the funding gap, then the outside share required at the revealed value versus the probability-weighted value.
Funding gap is $100 - 20 = 80$. Compare revealed share $80/200 = 40\%$ against pooled share $80 / (0.5\times 200 + 0.5\times 120) = 80/160 = 50\%$.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Outside financing = 80. With the high type credibly revealed, the share is 80 ÷ 200 = **40%**. Without revelation, expected payoff = 0.5 × 200 + 0.5 × 120 = 160, giving a **50%** share. Gross benefit to the high-type owner = (50% − 40%) × 200 = **20**. Under this simplified comparison the disclosure cost must be below 20 for a strictly positive net benefit; at 20 the owner is indifferent. Gross benefit is before reporting/audit costs.
questions.pitfall: Evaluating the 10% ownership saving on the pooled expected value (160) instead of the true high-type payoff (200).

obsidianLink.heading: 1.4 Reliable reporting and the outside ownership share

questions.title: D2 · Recover profit from equity.
questions.promptMarkdown: Opening equity is £40,000 and closing equity is £54,000. Owners contributed £6,000 and withdrew £9,000 during the period. Assume there are no other direct equity movements. Calculate profit and explain the signs.
rubricChecks: Set up equity roll-forward separating capital contributions (£6,000) and drawings (£9,000) from profit
Calculated Profit = £54,000 − £40,000 − £6,000 + £9,000 = £17,000 and explained both signs
hints: Write the equity roll-forward with contributions and drawings separate from profit.
Rearrange $\text{Equity}_1 = \text{Equity}_0 + \text{Profit} + \text{Contributions} - \text{Drawings}$ to isolate Profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Closing equity = opening equity + profit + contributions − drawings. Profit = £54,000 − £40,000 − £6,000 + £9,000 = **£17,000**. Remove contributions because they increased equity without being earned; add back drawings because they reduced equity without being an expense.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting drawings (£9,000) instead of adding them back when solving for earned profit.

pacing.rationale: Focused single-concept calculation (break-even, overhead rate, inventory method, or working-capital adjustment) targeting 5 min under exam conditions.

questions.title: D4 · Prepare all three statements.
questions.promptMarkdown: A new sole trader starts with no balances. During its first reporting period: the owner invests £20,000 cash; the business receives a £10,000 long-term bank loan; buys equipment for £12,000 cash; buys £6,000 inventory on supplier credit; sells goods costing £4,000 on credit for £10,000; collects £7,000 from customers; pays suppliers £2,500; pays £1,000 rent for the period; and records £1,200 depreciation. There are no other transactions, taxes, interest, drawings or valuation adjustments. Prepare an income statement, closing statement of financial position, and direct cash-flow statement. Explain the difference between profit and operating cash flow.
rubricChecks: Income statement: Revenue £10,000 − COGS £4,000 = Gross profit £6,000; less Rent £1,000 and Depreciation £1,200 = Profit £3,800
Statement of financial position: Bank £21,500 + AR £3,000 + Inv £2,000 + Equipment net £10,800 = Total Assets £37,300 = Liabilities £13,500 + Equity £23,800
Cash flow statement: Operating +£3,500, Investing −£12,000, Financing +£30,000 -> Net cash +£21,500
Explained profit (£3,800) vs operating cash (£3,500) via non-cash depreciation and working-capital timing
hints: Create separate ledgers for cash, receivables, inventory, equipment, payables and equity before making statements.

Reconcile operating cash flow both directly (£7,000 receipts − £2,500 supplier payments − £1,000 rent) and indirectly from Profit (£3,800) + Depreciation (£1,200) − ΔInv (£2,000) − ΔAR (£3,000) + ΔAP (£3,500).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Income statement:** Revenue £10,000 − cost of sales £4,000 = gross profit £6,000. Less rent £1,000 and depreciation £1,200 gives **profit £3,800**.

**Financial position:** Bank £21,500; receivables £3,000; inventory £2,000; equipment net of depreciation £10,800. **Total assets £37,300.** Supplier payables £3,500 and long-term loan £10,000 give liabilities £13,500. Equity is capital £20,000 + profit £3,800 = £23,800. Check: **£37,300 = £13,500 + £23,800**.

**Cash flows:** Operating = customer receipts £7,000 − suppliers £2,500 − rent £1,000 = **£3,500**. Investing = equipment **−£12,000**. Financing = capital £20,000 + loan £10,000 = **£30,000**. Net cash increase = **£21,500**, matching the bank balance.

**Profit-to-cash bridge:** £3,800 + depreciation £1,200 − inventory increase £2,000 − receivables increase £3,000 + payables increase £3,500 = **£3,500**. Capital and loans create financing cash rather than sales revenue. A loan principal repayment would reduce cash and the liability, rather than create an operating expense.
questions.pitfall: Treating owner capital (£20,000) or bank loan proceeds (£10,000) as revenue, or expensing the full £6,000 inventory purchase instead of £4,000 sold.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.1 Build the income statement in layers

pacing.rationale: Full multi-statement, T-account, cash-flow, or residual-income reconciliation requiring complete ledger/working-capital roll-forwards and balance checks.

questions.title: D3 · Record the sale.
questions.promptMarkdown: Under a perpetual inventory system, goods costing £1,200 are sold on credit for £2,000. Record both entries. The customer later pays £700. Record that entry and calculate the remaining receivable. Would omitting the entire sale necessarily make the trial balance disagree?
rubricChecks: Recorded credit sale: Dr Trade Receivables £2,000 / Cr Sales £2,000 AND Dr Cost of Sales £1,200 / Cr Inventory £1,200
Recorded partial collection: Dr Bank £700 / Cr Trade Receivables £700, leaving closing receivable £1,300
Explained that omitting an entire transaction leaves total debits equal to total credits, so the trial balance still agrees
hints: A perpetual-inventory credit sale needs a revenue/receivable entry and a separate cost/inventory entry.
After recording both legs of the credit sale (receivable/revenue at £2,000 and COGS/inventory at £1,200), deduct the £700 cash collection from receivables.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Debit receivables £2,000; credit sales £2,000. Debit cost of sales £1,200; credit inventory £1,200. On collection, debit bank £700; credit receivables £700. Receivable remaining = **£1,300**. Omitting both sides can leave a trial balance balanced; agreement alone is insufficient.
questions.pitfall: Recording only the £2,000 revenue entry under perpetual inventory and forgetting the simultaneous £1,200 cost-of-sales/inventory entry.

questions.title: D9 · Reconcile operating cash flow.
questions.promptMarkdown: Profit before tax after interest is £12,500. Depreciation is £3,000 and interest expense is £500. Inventories increase £1,000, receivables decrease £500 and payables increase £700. Cash interest, tax and dividends paid are £400, £2,000 and £600. Using this course's convention of deducting those three payments in operating activities, calculate cash generated from operations and net operating cash flow. Explain the three working-capital signs.
rubricChecks: Calculated Cash generated from operations = £16,200
Calculated Net cash from operating activities = £13,200 under course convention
Explained why inventory rises use cash (`−`) while receivable drops and payable rises release/preserve cash (`+`)
hints: Begin at the specified profit subtotal; do not confuse expense with cash paid.
Add back £3,000 depreciation and £500 interest expense to PBT (£12,500), apply `−1,000 + 500 + 700` working capital, then deduct cash interest/tax/dividends paid (`400 + 2,000 + 600`).
questions.solutionMarkdown: Cash generated = £12,500 + £3,000 + £500 − £1,000 + £500 + £700 = **£16,200**. Net operating cash = £16,200 − £400 − £2,000 − £600 = **£13,200**, using the stated course convention. Additional inventory ties up cash; lower receivables releases cash; higher payables preserves cash through deferred supplier payments. Explain policy choices if a question specifies a different cash-flow classification.
questions.pitfall: Deducting the £500 income-statement interest expense at the bottom instead of the £400 cash interest paid.

questions.title: D5 · Rebuild CVP from data.
questions.promptMarkdown: With unchanged price, unit variable cost and total fixed cost, a business sells 400 units for £32,000 and makes £8,000 profit. In a second period it sells 600 units for £48,000 and makes £18,000 profit. Find unit price, unit contribution, unit variable cost, fixed costs, break-even units and units needed for £20,000 profit. State one limitation of this model.
rubricChecks: Found unit price £80, unit contribution £50, unit variable cost £30, and fixed costs £12,000
Calculated Break-even = 240 units and Target volume for £20,000 profit = 640 units
Stated linear relevant-range / constant-mix limitation
hints: Subtract the two profit equations, then recover fixed cost from either period.
Divide $\Delta\text{Profit} = £18,000 - £8,000 = £10,000$ by $\Delta Q = 200$ units to get £50 unit contribution.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Price £80. Unit contribution = (£18,000 − £8,000) ÷ (600 − 400) = **£50**. Unit variable cost = £80 − £50 = **£30**. Fixed costs = 400 × £50 − £8,000 = **£12,000**. Break-even = £12,000 ÷ £50 = **240 units**. Target = (£12,000 + £20,000) ÷ £50 = **640 units**. These results depend on a relevant activity range with unchanged unit price, variable cost and fixed costs; capacity limits and product-mix changes can invalidate them.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting to add fixed costs (£12,000) to target profit (£20,000) in the target-volume numerator.

pacing.rationale: Medium multi-part numerical problem (scarce-resource ranking, ABC pool rates, or multi-year NPV schedule) calibrated to ~11 min fluent exam pace.

questions.title: D6 · Decide on a special order.
questions.promptMarkdown: An order for 500 units pays £40 per unit. Incremental variable cost is £36 per unit and accepting it creates a £1,500 one-off setup cost. Allocated existing fixed overhead is £12 per unit and will not change. First assume spare capacity and no effect on normal business. Calculate the profit effect and decide. Then calculate the effect if the same order also displaces £1,600 of normal contribution.
rubricChecks: Excluded the £12/unit unchanged existing fixed-overhead allocation
Spare capacity: $+£2,000 - £1,500 = +£500$ incremental profit -> Accept
Full capacity with £1,600 displaced contribution: $+£500 - £1,600 = -£1,100$ -> Reject
hints: Compare the extra revenue with changed outlays and contribution forgone. Existing allocations matter only if they change.
Incremental contribution before setup is $500 \times (£40 - £36) = £2,000$; deduct the £1,500 one-off setup cost, then test the £1,600 displaced contribution.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Incremental profit = 500 × (£40 − £36) − £1,500 = **+£500**. Accept under the stated spare-capacity and no-side-effects assumptions. Existing fixed allocations do not change. With displaced normal contribution, the effect becomes £500 − £1,600 = **−£1,100**; reject on those financial assumptions.
questions.pitfall: Including the £12/unit allocated existing fixed overhead as if accepting the order increased general fixed costs.

pacing.rationale: Focused single-concept calculation (break-even, overhead rate, inventory method, or working-capital adjustment) targeting 5 min under exam conditions.

questions.title: D7 · Use scarce capacity.
questions.promptMarkdown: Product A sells for £80, has variable cost £30 and uses five scarce hours per unit. Product B sells for £100, has variable cost £60 and uses two hours per unit. There are 120 hours available; maximum demand is 40 units of A and 30 of B. With divisible production and unchanged fixed costs, choose the production quantities and calculate total contribution. Explain why ranking by contribution per unit would mislead.
rubricChecks: Computed contribution per scarce hour: B = £20/hr (1st) vs A = £10/hr (2nd)
Optimal plan: 30 units of B (60 hrs) + 12 units of A (60 hrs) = Total contribution £1,800
Explained why ranking by per-unit contribution (£50 > £40) wastes constrained capacity
hints: Find contribution per scarce hour, then apply each demand limit.
Contribution per scarce hour is $£50 / 5\text{h} = £10$/h for A vs $£40 / 2\text{h} = £20$/h for B — max out B's 30-unit demand first!
questions.solutionMarkdown: A contributes £50 per unit, but £10 per scarce hour. B contributes £40 per unit, but £20 per scarce hour. Make **30 B**, using 60 hours, then **12 A**, using the remaining 60. Total contribution = 30 × £40 + 12 × £50 = **£1,800**. Higher contribution per unit does not necessarily use constrained capacity better. This ranking assumes a single binding constraint and the stated divisibility and demand limits.
questions.pitfall: Producing 24 units of A first (120 hrs -> £1,200 contribution) and losing £600 of contribution.

questions.title: D8 · Apply ABC.
questions.promptMarkdown: Setup overhead is £24,000 for 120 setups. Inspection overhead is £18,000 for 600 inspections. A job uses three setups and ten inspections and has £5,000 direct cost. Find both driver rates, assigned overhead and full job cost. Explain why a single labour-hour allocation could produce a different result.
rubricChecks: Calculated driver rates: £200/setup and £30/inspection
Assigned job overhead = `3(£200) + 10(£30) = £900` and full job cost = £5,900
Explained how single labour-hour absorption distorts batch/setup-intensive jobs
hints: Compute one rate for each activity pool and multiply by the job’s usage.
Setup rate = $£24,000 / 120$; Inspection rate = $£18,000 / 600$; add both activity charges to the £5,000 direct cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Setup rate = £24,000 ÷ 120 = **£200/setup**. Inspection rate = £18,000 ÷ 600 = **£30/inspection**. Assigned overhead = 3 × £200 + 10 × £30 = **£900**. Full job cost = **£5,900**. A labour-hour rate assigns costs by a different activity measure and can overcharge or undercharge a job whose setup/inspection use is disproportionate to its labour hours.
questions.pitfall: Reporting assigned overhead (£900) as total job cost and omitting the £5,000 direct cost.

questions.title: D10 · Compare investment methods.
questions.promptMarkdown: A machine costs £40,000, lasts four years, has no residual value or working capital, and generates £14,000 net cash inflow at each year end. Use 10% cost of capital and straight-line depreciation; ignore tax. Calculate ARR using average investment, payback, NPV at 10% and at 20%, and an interpolated IRR. For payback only, assume cash accrues uniformly within the recovery year. Recommend a decision and distinguish the approximate IRR from a solved IRR.
rubricChecks: Computed ARR = 20% (£4,000 / £20,000) and continuous Payback = 2.86 years (`40,000 / 14,000`)
Interpolated IRR ≈ 15.38% (vs solved 14.96%) and noted non-linearity over wide rate intervals
hints: Use profit after depreciation for ARR and cash for the other methods. Put residual cash at the right date.
Annual depreciation is $£40,000/4 = £10,000$ (so annual profit = £4,000 on £20,000 average investment); for NPV/IRR/Payback use the £14,000 cash inflows!
questions.solutionMarkdown: Annual depreciation £10,000; annual profit £4,000; average investment £20,000. **ARR 20%. Payback 2.857 years** under the within-year assumption. NPV = −£40,000 + the four discounted £14,000 inflows: **+£4,378.12 at 10%** and **−£3,757.72 at 20%**. Linear interpolation gives 10% + [4,378.12 ÷ (4,378.12 + 3,757.72)] × 10 percentage points = **15.38%**. A numerical solution gives approximately **14.96%**; interpolation over a wide interval is approximate. Accept at a 10% required return because NPV is positive. ARR uses accounting profit, while NPV, IRR and payback use cash flows; ordinary payback also ignores cash flows after recovery.
questions.pitfall: Discounting the £4,000 accounting profit instead of the £14,000 net cash inflow in NPV.

questions.title: D11 · Connect profit to value.
questions.promptMarkdown: For Q10 calculate opening operating assets, accounting profit, capital charge and residual income in each year. Discount residual income at 10% and compare it with NPV. State the assumptions behind the equality.
questions.contextMarkdown: **Context (from D10):** A machine costs £40,000 at $t=0$, lasts 4 years with zero residual value and straight-line depreciation (£10,000/yr), and generates £14,000 net cash inflow at the end of each year ($r = 10\%$, annual profit = £4,000, $\text{NPV}_{10\%} = +£4,378.12$).
rubricChecks: Computed annual capital charges (`£4k, £3k, £2k, £1k`) and Residual Incomes (`£0, £1,000, £2,000, £3,000`)
Discounted RIs at 10% to **+£4,378.12**, matching $\text{NPV}_{10\%}$ to the penny
Stated Preinreich–Lücke conditions: clean-surplus profit, opening-asset capital charge at $r$, and zero terminal operating assets
hints: Deduct the capital charge on opening operating assets from each year’s accounting profit.
Opening operating assets step down by £10,000 straight-line depreciation each year (`40k, 30k, 20k, 10k`), so the 10% capital charge drops by £1,000/yr (`4k, 3k, 2k, 1k`).
questions.solutionMarkdown: Opening operating assets: **£40,000; £30,000; £20,000; £10,000**. Annual profit: £4,000. Capital charges: **£4,000; £3,000; £2,000; £1,000**. Residual incomes: **£0; £1,000; £2,000; £3,000**. Their discounted sum at 10% is **£4,378.12**, matching NPV. The equality here uses clean-surplus accounting, matching cash and accounting flows, the same discount rate, and zero terminal operating assets.
questions.pitfall: Charging the 10% capital charge on closing book value instead of opening operating assets.

questions.solutionMarkdown: Editorial solution (£m). Cash generated = PBT 25 + interest 4 + depreciation 22 − inventory increase 1 + receivable decrease 1 − payable decrease 3 = **48**. questions.title: WFA-M1 · Fundamental qualitative characteristics
questions.promptMarkdown: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which pair represents the two **fundamental** qualitative characteristics of useful financial information?
hints: Distinguish fundamental qualities from the four enhancing qualities.
Information must both matter to decisions and accurately depict economic substance.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Relevance** and **faithful representation** are the two fundamental qualitative characteristics; comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability are *enhancing* characteristics.
questions.pitfall: Confusing enhancing characteristics (comparability/verifiability) with fundamental characteristics.

questions.title: WFA-M2 · Asset recognition criteria on the SFP
questions.promptMarkdown: Nordic Design AS spends £40,000 training its sales staff on a new CRM system. How should this £40,000 expenditure be treated in the financial statements?
options: Capitalised as an intangible non-current asset and amortised over 5 years
Recognised immediately as an expense in the income statement because the firm lacks legal control over staff remaining
Recorded directly as a deduction from share capital without passing through profit
Held in current assets as prepaid employee goodwill
hints: Check the control test for an asset in Chapter 2.
Employees can resign, so future economic benefits from general training are not controlled by the entity.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Because the business cannot **control** employees' future service, staff training fails the asset recognition test and is expensed immediately in the income statement.
questions.pitfall: Capitalising internally incurred staff training or marketing spend as an intangible asset.

questions.title: WFA-M3 · Double-entry effect of credit purchase settlement
questions.promptMarkdown: When a business pays £12,000 from its bank account to settle an existing trade payable (with no settlement discount), what is the double-entry effect?
options: Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Cash at bank £12,000; Credit Trade payables £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Purchases expense £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity decreases)
Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Retained earnings £12,000 (equity increases)
hints: Decreasing a liability is a Debit; decreasing an asset is a Credit.
Was any revenue earned or new expense incurred at the moment of cash settlement?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Paying a supplier reduces the liability **Trade payables** (**Debit £12,000**) and reduces the asset **Cash at bank** (**Credit £12,000**). Total assets and total liabilities fall equally; profit and equity are unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Treating supplier cash payment as an expense at settlement rather than when goods/services were incurred.

questions.title: WFA-M4 · Accrued expense adjustment error
questions.promptMarkdown: If an accountant forgets to record £8,500 of accrued electricity expense at year-end, what is the effect on the year-end financial statements?
options: Profit is understated by £8,500 and current liabilities are overstated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and current liabilities are understated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and cash is overstated by £8,500
Assets are overstated by £8,500 and liabilities are unaffected
hints: Write the missing entry: Dr Electricity expense £8,500, Cr Accruals (current liability) £8,500.
Omitting an expense makes profit too high; omitting the accrual makes liabilities too low.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Omitting an accrued expense leaves expenses £8,500 too low (**profit & equity overstated by £8,500**) and omits the current liability (**current liabilities understated by £8,500**). Cash is unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Assuming accrued expenses affect the year-end cash balance.

questions.title: WFA-M6 · Relevant cost of inventory already in stock
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm holds 400 kg of Specialty Alloy bought last year for £15/kg (historic cost £6,000). If not used on a one-off contract, it would be sold immediately as scrap for £9/kg; the alloy has no other use in the business. What is the relevant cost of using the 400 kg on the contract?
options: £0, because the alloy is already paid for
hints: Sunk purchase cost (£15/kg) is always irrelevant.
Ask what cash inflow the firm sacrifices by using the material instead of scrapping it.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: The historic £6,000 is sunk. Using the alloy sacrifices £9/kg in immediate scrap proceeds, so the relevant opportunity cost is $400 \times £9 = \mathbf{£3,600}$.
questions.pitfall: Treating existing material as free (£0) and ignoring its forgone scrap proceeds.

questions.title: WFA-M7 · Operating gearing and profit sensitivity
questions.promptMarkdown: Company H has high fixed costs and low variable cost per unit; Company L has low fixed costs and high variable cost per unit. At the same current sales volume and operating profit, if sales volume rises by 15%:
options: Company L's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage than Company H's
Company H's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage because its contribution margin ratio is higher
Both companies will experience the exact same 15% increase in operating profit
Company H has a lower break-even point when demand falls
hints: Recall operating gearing = Contribution / Operating profit.
High fixed costs with equal profit imply a larger total contribution, magnifying volume swings.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Company H has higher **operating gearing**: each extra unit sold generates a higher contribution while fixed costs stay constant, so profit rises (and falls) by a larger percentage than at Company L.
questions.pitfall: Mixing up operating gearing risk on the downside with profit sensitivity on the upside.

questions.title: WFA-M8 · Traditional volume-based costing vs ABC cross-subsidisation
questions.promptMarkdown: When a multi-product factory switches from a single direct-labour-hour (DLH) overhead rate to Activity-Based Costing (ABC), low-volume complex batch products typically show:
options: A lower unit cost under ABC because they consume fewer total labour hours
A higher unit cost under ABC because batch-level set-up and inspection costs are spread over fewer units
Unchanged unit cost, because total factory overhead is identical
Zero indirect cost, because ABC only traces direct materials
hints: Traditional DLH allocates set-up/inspection pools in proportion to volume.
Small complex batches trigger disproportionate set-ups per unit produced.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Traditional volume-based rates **under-cost** low-volume complex products and **over-cost** high-volume standard products; ABC assigns batch-level set-ups/inspections accurately, raising the reported unit cost of small complex batches.
questions.pitfall: Assuming fewer total DLHs means complex small batches become cheaper under ABC.

questions.title: WFA-M9 · Mutually exclusive projects: NPV vs IRR
questions.promptMarkdown: Projects X (initial outlay £50,000, IRR 22%, NPV +£14,000) and Y (initial outlay £200,000, IRR 17%, NPV +£29,000) are mutually exclusive at a 10% cost of capital with no capital rationing. To maximise shareholder wealth, the firm should:
options: Accept Project X because 22% IRR exceeds 17% IRR
Accept Project Y because it generates the higher positive Net Present Value (+£29,000)
Accept both X and Y because both have positive NPVs
Reject both until their IRRs are equal
hints: IRR is a percentage rate and ignores project scale.
Which metric directly measures absolute shareholder wealth added in today's pounds?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **NPV** directly measures absolute wealth creation in present-value monetary terms (+£29,000 vs +£14,000). For mutually exclusive projects, IRR suffers from the **scale problem**.
questions.pitfall: Ranking mutually exclusive projects of different sizes by IRR percentage instead of NPV.

questions.title: WFA-M10 · Working capital in NPV cash-flow schedules
questions.promptMarkdown: A 4-year project requires £25,000 of net working capital at $t = 0$, maintained throughout Years 1–4 and fully recovered at the end of Year 4 ($t = 4$) at a 10% discount rate. What is the net effect of working capital on the project's **NPV**?
options: £0, because −£25,000 at t=0 and +£25,000 at t=4 cancel out
Negative (−£7,924.66), because the t=4 recovery is discounted while the t=0 outflow is not
Negative (−£25,000), because working capital release is an accounting entry rather than cash
Positive (+£17,075.34), because working capital recovery adds to Year 4 profit
hints: Time value of money means tying up cash for 4 years carries an opportunity cost.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: In undiscounted terms $-25,000 + 25,000 = 0$, but in present value $-25,000 + 25,000 / 1.10^4 = -25,000 + 17,075.34 = \mathbf{-£7,924.66}$. Tying up working capital reduces NPV by the lost time value.
questions.pitfall: Omitting the t=4 working capital release OR claiming t=0 and t=4 cancel in PV terms.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-E1 · Nordic Craft Ltd · FIFO, Accruals, Income Statement & Equity (45 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Nordic Craft Ltd** has extracted the following information for the financial year ended **31 December 2026** (all currency figures in GBP):

| Item | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Credit sales revenue | 420,000 |
| Irrecoverable trade receivables written off during 2026 | 4,000 |
| Cash wages paid during 2026 | 140,000 |
| Unpaid December wages accrued at 31 Dec 2026 | 6,000 |
| Cash rent paid during 2026 (includes 8,000 prepaid for Jan–Feb 2027) | 48,000 |
| Other cash operating expenses | 55,000 |
| Loan interest expense | 10,000 |
| Opening total equity (1 Jan 2026) | 250,000 |
| Cash dividends paid during 2026 (no new shares issued) | 30,000 |

**Inventory batches (FIFO cost flow — 800 units sold during 2026):**

| Date | Description | Units | Unit Cost | Total |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 Jan 2026 | Opening inventory | 200 | 40 | 8,000 |
| 14 Apr 2026 | Purchase | 500 | 44 | 22,000 |
| 9 Oct 2026 | Purchase | 400 | 50 | 20,000 |
| **Total available** | | **1,100** | | **50,000** |

**Non-current assets:** Workshop equipment was acquired for **120,000** with an estimated residual value of **20,000** and a useful life of **5 years** (straight-line depreciation).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Under rising unit purchase prices, FIFO reports a higher closing inventory value and higher profit than AVCO.
   - **b.** Paying a cash dividend to shareholders is recorded as an operating expense in the income statement.
   - **c.** Prepaid rent at year-end is classified as a current asset on the Statement of Financial Position.
2. Using the **FIFO** method, calculate: (i) Closing inventory at 31 Dec 2026 *(5 points)*, (ii) Cost of sales (COGS) for 2026 *(5 points)*, and (iii) Gross profit *(5 points)*. *(15 points in total)*
3. Calculate the adjusted 2026 figures for: (i) Wages expense *(4 points)*, (ii) Rent expense *(4 points)*, (iii) Annual straight-line depreciation *(3 points)*, (iv) Operating profit (EBIT) *(4 points)*, and (v) Net profit for the year *(3 points)*. *(18 points in total)*
4. Calculate Closing Total Equity on the Statement of Financial Position at 31 Dec 2026. *(6 points)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. FIFO vs AVCO under rising prices
1b. Cash dividends are an income statement expense
1c. Prepaid rent is a current asset on the SFP
Closing Inventory at 31 Dec (300 units under FIFO)
Cost of Sales (COGS) for 2026
Gross Profit
2026 Wages Expense (incl. year-end accrual)
2026 Rent Expense (after prepayment adjustment)
2026 Annual Straight-Line Depreciation
Operating Profit (EBIT)
Net Profit for the Year (after interest)

wiseflowFields.group: 4. Statement of Financial Position Equity (6 pts)
wiseflowFields.label: Closing Total Equity at 31 Dec 2026

hints: Under FIFO, the 800 sold units use all 200 opening units (@£40), all 500 April units (@£44), and 100 October units (@£50), leaving 300 October units in closing inventory.

Add accrued wages (+£6,000), deduct prepaid rent (−£8,000), deduct straight-line depreciation ((120,000 − 20,000)/5 = £20,000) and bad debts (£4,000). Dividends reduce Retained Earnings directly, not Net Profit.
rubricChecks: Computed FIFO closing inventory (£15,000) and COGS (£35,000)
Adjusted wages (£146,000) and rent (£40,000) accurately under accruals
Kept dividends (£30,000) out of Net Profit (£110,000) and rolled forward Equity (£330,000)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E1 (45 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(dividends are an appropriation of retained earnings, not an expense)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **FIFO Inventory & Gross Profit:**
   - Available goods $= 8,000 + 22,000 + 20,000 = £50,000$ ($1,100$ units). Closing units $= 1,100 - 800 = 300$ units from 9 Oct batch $@ £50 = \mathbf{£15,000}$.
   - $\text{COGS} = 50,000 - 15,000 = \mathbf{£35,000}$ *(check: $200(40) + 500(44) + 100(50) = 8,000 + 22,000 + 5,000 = 35,000$)*.
   - $\text{Gross Profit} = 420,000 - 35,000 = \mathbf{£385,000}$.
3. **Operating & Net Profit:**
   - Wages expense $= 140,000 + 6,000 = \mathbf{£146,000}$ · Rent expense $= 48,000 - 8,000 = \mathbf{£40,000}$ · Depreciation $= (120,000 - 20,000)/5 = \mathbf{£20,000}$.
   - Total operating expenses $= 146,000 + 40,000 + 20,000 + 4,000 + 55,000 = £265,000 \implies \text{Operating Profit} = 385,000 - 265,000 = \mathbf{£120,000}$.
   - $\text{Net Profit} = 120,000 - 10,000 = \mathbf{£110,000}$.
4. **Closing Equity:** $250,000 + 110,000 - 30,000 = \mathbf{£330,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting dividends inside Net Profit, or forgetting to subtract residual value (£20,000) in straight-line depreciation.

pacing.rationale: 45-point WISEflow FLOWmulti exercise (45m exam par at 1 pt = 1 min; ±2% rounding margin).

questions.title: WFA-E2 · Bergen Marine Ltd · Indirect Statement of Cash Flows (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
The following summary financial information has been extracted for **Bergen Marine Ltd** for the financial year ended **31 December 2026** (all figures in **£m**; use a minus sign `-` for net outflows and negative balances):

| Statement / Balance Item | 1 Jan 2026 | 31 Dec 2026 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Property, plant & equipment (carrying amount / NBV) | 210 | 236 |
| Inventories | 30 | 39 |
| Trade receivables | 45 | 41 |
| Trade payables | 28 | 22 |
| Tax payable | 14 | 11 |
| Cash / (bank overdraft) | −10 | ? |

**Additional information for 2026 (£m):**

- **a)** Operating profit (EBIT) was **84**, stated after charging depreciation of **26** and a **loss on disposal** of equipment of **5**.
- **b)** The disposed equipment had a carrying amount (NBV) of **18** and was sold for **13** cash. All PPE additions were paid in cash.
- **c)** Interest paid in cash was **8**. Income statement tax charge was **16**.
- **d)** A new long-term bank loan of **20** was raised, and cash dividends of **12** were paid (classified under **Financing activities**).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** A non-cash loss on disposal of non-current assets is added back to operating profit when reconciling to cash generated from operations, while the actual sale proceeds appear under investing activities.
   - **b.** Making a bonus issue of shares (capitalising reserves) generates a financing cash inflow.
   - **c.** Profitable rapidly growing firms can experience negative operating cash flows (overtrading) if working capital expands faster than cash profits.
2. Calculate: (i) Cash generated from operations before interest & tax *(5 points)*, (ii) Cash tax paid during 2026 *(4 points)*, and (iii) Net cash from operating activities *(4 points)*. *(13 points in total)*
3. Calculate: (i) Cash paid for PPE additions *(4 points)*, (ii) Net cash from investing activities *(4 points)*, and (iii) Net cash from financing activities *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
4. Calculate the closing cash balance at 31 December 2026. *(4 points)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Disposal loss add-back & investing proceeds
1b. Bonus share issue creates financing cash inflow
1c. Profitable growth can cause negative operating cash flow (overtrading)
Cash Generated from Operations (before interest & tax)
Cash Tax Paid during 2026 (enter positive magnitude 19 or -19)
Net Cash from Operating Activities (after interest 8 & tax paid)
Cash Paid for PPE Additions (magnitude 70 or -70)
Net Cash from Investing Activities (use minus sign)
Net Cash from Financing Activities
Closing Cash Balance at 31 Dec 2026

hints: Cash generated = Operating profit (84) + Depreciation (26) + Disposal loss (5) − ΔInventory (9) + ΔReceivables decrease (4) − ΔPayables decrease (6).
Roll forward PPE NBV: Opening (210) + Additions − Disposal NBV (18) − Depreciation (26) = Closing (236) ⇒ Additions = 70. Net investing = −70 + 13 disposal cash = −57.
rubricChecks: Added back both depreciation (26) and loss on disposal (5) in Operating cash
Reconciled Tax Paid (14 + 16 − 11 = 19) and PPE Additions (70) via roll-forward
Combined Opening Overdraft (−10) + Net Change (+28) = +18 Closing Cash
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(a bonus issue transfers reserves to share capital with zero cash flow)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Operating Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{Cash generated} = 84 + 26 + 5 - (39 - 30) + (45 - 41) - (28 - 22) = 115 - 9 + 4 - 6 = \mathbf{104}$.
   - $\text{Tax paid} = 14 + 16 - 11 = \mathbf{19}$.
   - $\text{Net cash from operating activities} = 104 - 8 - 19 = \mathbf{77}$.
3. **Investing & Financing Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{PPE Additions} = 236 - 210 + 18 + 26 = \mathbf{70} \implies \text{Net investing cash flow} = -70 + 13 = \mathbf{-57}$.
   - $\text{Net financing cash flow} = +20\text{ (loan)} - 12\text{ (dividends)} = \mathbf{+8}$.
4. **Closing Cash:** Net change $= 77 - 57 + 8 = +28 \implies -10 + 28 = \mathbf{+18\text{ (£m)}}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting disposal loss instead of adding it back, or forgetting disposal NBV (18) and depreciation (26) when solving for PPE additions.

questions.title: WFA-E3 · Oslo Mobility · Break-Even, Margin of Safety & Scarce Machine Hours (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Oslo Mobility Ltd** manufactures electric bicycles. Budgeted data for its existing **Commuter** model and a proposed **Cargo** model are shown below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Metric | Commuter | Cargo (Part B) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Selling price per unit | 500 | 750 |
| Variable cost per unit | 300 | 450 |
| Budgeted monthly sales (Part A) | 800 units | — |
| Maximum monthly market demand (Part B) | 600 units | 300 units |
| Specialised CNC machine time per unit | 2.5 MH | 5.0 MH |

Total monthly fixed costs are **120,000** in both Part A and Part B. In **Part B**, specialised CNC machine capacity is limited to **2,100 machine hours (MH)** per month.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Margin of safety (%) measures the percentage by which budgeted sales can fall before the business incurs an operating loss.
   - **b.** When machine hours are the single scarce limiting factor, products should be ranked by highest contribution per unit of output.
   - **c.** An increase in the income tax rate raises the pre-tax sales volume required to earn a specified **after-tax** target profit.
2. **Part A (Single-product Commuter):** Calculate: (i) Break-even sales volume in units *(4 points)*, (ii) Margin of safety as a % of budgeted sales *(4 points)*, and (iii) Monthly units required to earn an operating profit of 70,000 *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
3. **Part B (Scarce CNC capacity of 2,100 MH):** Calculate: (i) Commuter contribution per machine hour *(4 points)*, (ii) Optimal monthly units of Cargo to produce *(4 points)*, and (iii) Maximum monthly operating profit under the optimal mix *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Definition of Margin of Safety (%)
1b. Scarce factor ranking uses contribution per unit of output
1c. Higher tax rate increases volume needed for an after-tax target profit

hints: Unit CM for Commuter = £500 − £300 = £200. Margin of safety % = (Budgeted − BEP) / Budgeted × 100.
Rank by CM per scarce machine hour: Commuter = £200 / 2.5 MH = £80/MH vs Cargo = £300 / 5.0 MH = £60/MH. Fulfil Commuter's 600-unit demand first!
rubricChecks: Calculated BEP (600 units), MOS (25%), and target-profit volume (950 units)
Ranked Commuter (£80/MH) ahead of Cargo (£60/MH) despite Cargo's larger £300 unit CM
Allocated remaining 600 MH to 120 Cargo units for £36,000 maximum profit
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E3 (30 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(rank by contribution **per unit of the scarce resource**, £/MH)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Part A (CVP):**
   - $\text{BEP} = 120,000 / (500 - 300) = \mathbf{600\text{ units}}$.
   - $\text{Margin of Safety \%} = (800 - 600)/800 \times 100 = \mathbf{25\%}$.
   - $\text{Target units} = (120,000 + 70,000)/200 = \mathbf{950\text{ units}}$.
3. **Part B (Scarce Machine Hours):**
   - Commuter: $£200 / 2.5\text{ MH} = \mathbf{£80/\text{MH}}$ (Rank 1) · Cargo: $£300 / 5.0\text{ MH} = £60/\text{MH}$ (Rank 2).
   - Produce max **600 Commuter** units ($600 \times 2.5 = 1,500\text{ MH}$). Remaining capacity $= 2,100 - 1,500 = 600\text{ MH} \implies 600 / 5.0 = \mathbf{120\text{ Cargo units}}$.
   - $\text{Max Operating Profit} = 600(200) + 120(300) - 120,000 = 120,000 + 36,000 - 120,000 = \mathbf{£36,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Dividing Margin of Safety by BEP (600) instead of budgeted sales (800), or prioritising Cargo because £300 > £200 per unit.

questions.title: WFA-E4 · Fjord Tech · NPV, Working Capital Recovery, Payback & ARR (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Fjord Tech AS** is evaluating a 4-year capital investment project with a cost of capital of **r = 10%**. Projected cash flows and asset data are summarized below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Period | Item | Amount |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| t = 0 | Equipment purchase outlay | −160,000 |
| t = 0 | Immediate working capital outlay (fully recovered at t = 4) | −20,000 |
| t = 1 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 55,000 |
| t = 2 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 65,000 |
| t = 3 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 60,000 |
| t = 4 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 50,000 |
| t = 4 | Expected equipment disposal (salvage) value | 20,000 |

Equipment is depreciated on a straight-line basis over 4 years (annual depreciation = **35,000**; average equipment carrying value = **90,000**). *(10% discount factors: t = 1: `0.9091`, t = 2: `0.8264`, t = 3: `0.7513`, t = 4: `0.6830`.)*

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Depreciation is a non-cash expense and must not be deducted from cash flows in an NPV schedule, though it reduces accounting profit in ARR.
   - **b.** Financing interest charges on loans used to fund the project should be subtracted as an annual cash outflow in the project's cash-flow line before discounting at the cost of capital.
   - **c.** Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) ignores the timing of cash flows within the project's life.
2. Calculate: (i) Total initial cash outflow at t = 0 (use minus sign) *(4 points)*, (ii) Total terminal cash inflow at t = 4 *(4 points)*, and (iii) Undiscounted payback period in years *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
3. Calculate: (i) Net Present Value (NPV) at 10% *(6 points)*, (ii) Average annual operating profit after depreciation *(3 points)*, and (iii) Accounting Rate of Return (ARR %) on average equipment investment *(3 points)*. *(12 points in total)*

1b. Deduct loan interest in cash flows AND discount at cost of capital
1c. ARR ignores time value / cash flow timing
Total Initial Cash Outflow at t = 0 (incl. WC; use minus sign)
Total Terminal Cash Inflow in t = 4 (operating + salvage + WC release)
Undiscounted Payback Period (in years)

hints: At t=0 combine −£160,000 equipment and −£20,000 working capital (= −£180,000). At t=4 combine £50,000 operating + £20,000 salvage + £20,000 working capital recovery (= +£90,000).
Cumulative cash flow after Year 3 is −180,000 + 55,000 + 65,000 + 60,000 = 0! Discounting at 10% accounts for financing costs, so never double-count interest.
rubricChecks: Included £20,000 working capital outflow at t=0 and recovery at t=4
Computed exact NPV (+£30,262.28, or +£30,215 with 3-dec factors — both within ±2%)
Computed straight-line depreciation (£35,000/yr), average profit (£22,500), and ARR (25.0%)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E4 (30 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(discounting at the cost of capital already prices financing costs; deducting interest double-counts financing)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Cash Flows, Payback & NPV (10%):**
   - $CF_0 = -160,000 - 20,000 = \mathbf{-£180,000}$ · $CF_1 = 55,000$ · $CF_2 = 65,000$ · $CF_3 = 60,000$ · $CF_4 = 50,000 + 20,000 + 20,000 = \mathbf{+£90,000}$.
   - **Payback:** Cumulative cash after Year 3 $= -180,000 + 55,000 + 65,000 + 60,000 = 0 \implies \mathbf{3.00\text{ years}}$.
   - **NPV (exact):** $-180,000 + 55,000/1.1 + 65,000/1.21 + 60,000/1.331 + 90,000/1.4641 = \mathbf{£30,269.11}$ *(3-dec table factors give £30,215.00, well inside ±2% tolerance)*.
3. **ARR:** Annual depreciation $= (160,000 - 20,000)/4 = £35,000$. Average annual operating profit $= 57,500 - 35,000 = \mathbf{£22,500}$. On average equipment investment $(160,000 + 20,000)/2 = £90,000$, $\text{ARR} = 22,500 / 90,000 = \mathbf{25.0\%}$ *(or 20.45% if £20,000 WC is added to the denominator)*.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting working capital recovery (+£20,000) in t=4 or deducting £35,000 depreciation inside NPV cash flows.

questions.title: WFB-M4 · Reducing-balance depreciation in Year 2
questions.promptMarkdown: A delivery truck costs £80,000 with an estimated residual value of £10,000 and is depreciated using the **reducing-balance method at 25% per annum**. What is the depreciation charge in **Year 2**?

questions.title: WFB-M10 · Real vs nominal cash flows and discount rates
questions.promptMarkdown: When evaluating capital projects in the presence of general inflation, the golden consistency rule requires:
options: Discounting nominal (money) cash flows at the real cost of capital
Discounting real cash flows at the nominal (money) cost of capital
Either discounting nominal cash flows at the nominal rate OR real cash flows at the real rate (both give the exact same NPV)
Ignoring inflation completely because sales prices and costs never change
hints: Recall Fisher's relation $(1 + m) = (1 + r)(1 + i)$.
Match nominal with nominal, or real with real — never mix them!
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Consistency demands matching **nominal cash flows with the nominal discount rate** OR **real cash flows with the real discount rate**; via $(1+m)=(1+r)(1+i)$ both yield the identical NPV.
questions.pitfall: Discounting uninflated (real) cash flows using an inflation-loaded nominal WACC, which systematically understates NPV.

questions.title: WFB-E1 · Viken Retail · Reducing-Balance Depreciation, Asset Disposal & Doubtful Debts (40 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Viken Retail AS** is finalizing its financial statements for the year ended **31 December 2026**. The following balances and year-end adjustments apply (all currency figures in GBP):

| Account / Item | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Delivery fleet — original cost (1 Jan 2026, before transactions) | 200,000 |
| Delivery fleet — accumulated depreciation (1 Jan 2026) | 72,000 |
| Delivery fleet — opening carrying amount / NBV (1 Jan 2026) | 128,000 |
| Gross trade receivables (31 Dec 2026, before write-offs) | 95,000 |
| Opening allowance for doubtful debts (1 Jan 2026) | 2,600 |
| Draft operating profit (before adjustments a–c below) | 145,000 |

**Additional transactions and policies for 2026:**

- **a)** On **1 January 2026**, Viken sold an older van (original cost **50,000**, accumulated depreciation **28,000**) for **17,000** cash, and immediately purchased a replacement van for **54,000** cash.
- **b)** All vehicles are depreciated at **25% per annum reducing-balance** on the year-end carrying amount prior to 2026 depreciation.
- **c)** At **31 December 2026**, a bankrupt customer owing **5,000** is written off as irrecoverable, and the closing allowance for doubtful debts is set at **4%** of remaining trade receivables.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Changing depreciation method purely to hit a management bonus target violates faithful representation unless the pattern of economic benefit consumption genuinely changed.
   - **b.** Accumulated depreciation represents a ring-fenced cash fund set aside in the bank to buy replacement machinery.
   - **c.** Increasing the allowance for doubtful debts reduces both reported profit and net current assets.
2. For the delivery fleet, calculate: (i) Gain (+) or loss (−) on van disposal *(5 points)*, (ii) 2026 reducing-balance depreciation expense *(6 points)*, and (iii) Closing fleet carrying amount (NBV) at 31 Dec 2026 *(5 points)*. *(16 points in total)*
3. For trade receivables and profit, calculate: (i) Closing allowance for doubtful debts *(4 points)*, (ii) Total 2026 bad & doubtful debts expense *(4 points)*, (iii) Net trade receivables on the 31 Dec 2026 SFP *(4 points)*, and (iv) Adjusted 2026 operating profit *(6 points)*. *(18 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Depreciation method reflects economic consumption, not bonus smoothing
1b. Accumulated depreciation is a cash replacement fund
1c. Higher doubtful-debt allowance lowers profit and net current assets
Gain (+) or Loss (−) on Van Disposal (use minus sign for loss)
2026 Reducing-Balance Depreciation Expense (25%)
Closing Fleet Carrying Amount (NBV) at 31 Dec 2026
Closing Allowance for Doubtful Debts (4% of remaining receivables)
Total 2026 Bad & Doubtful Debts Expense in Income Statement
Net Trade Receivables Reported on 31 Dec 2026 SFP
Adjusted 2026 Operating Profit

hints: Disposed van NBV = £50,000 − £28,000 = £22,000; sold for £17,000 ⇒ −£5,000 loss. Active fleet NBV before 2026 depreciation = (£128,000 − £22,000) + £54,000 = £160,000.

Write off £5,000 first so remaining receivables = £90,000. Closing allowance = 4% × £90,000 = £3,600 (only the £1,000 increase over £2,600 opening allowance is an extra expense alongside the £5,000 write-off!).
rubricChecks: Calculated van disposal loss (−£5,000), 2026 depreciation (£40,000), and closing NBV (£120,000)
Charged £5,000 write-off + £1,000 allowance increase = £6,000 total expense (not £8,600!)
Reconciled final operating profit (£94,000) and net receivables (£86,400)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFB-E1 (40 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(depreciation is book cost allocation, not cash)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Fleet Disposal & Depreciation:**
   - Disposed NBV $= 50,000 - 28,000 = £22,000 \implies \text{Disposal result} = 17,000 - 22,000 = \mathbf{-£5,000}$ (loss).
   - Depreciable base $= (128,000 - 22,000) + 54,000 = £160,000 \implies \text{2026 Depreciation} = 0.25 \times 160,000 = \mathbf{£40,000}$.
   - Closing fleet NBV $= 160,000 - 40,000 = \mathbf{£120,000}$.
3. **Receivables & Operating Profit:**
   - Remaining gross receivables $= 95,000 - 5,000 = £90,000 \implies \text{Closing allowance} = 0.04 \times 90,000 = \mathbf{£3,600}$.
   - Income statement charge $= £5,000\text{ (write-off)} + (£3,600 - £2,600)\text{ (Δallowance)} = \mathbf{£6,000}$.
   - Net SFP receivables $= 90,000 - 3,600 = \mathbf{£86,400}$.
   - Adjusted Operating Profit $= 145,000 - 5,000 - 40,000 - 6,000 = \mathbf{£94,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Expensing the entire £3,600 closing allowance instead of the £1,000 movement above £2,600 opening allowance.

questions.title: WFB-E2 · Stavanger Engineering · Relevant Costing & Minimum Contract Price (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Stavanger Engineering AS** has been offered a fixed contract price of **23,500** for a one-off subsea valve order. The resources required for the contract are summarized below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Resource | Requirement | Current Status & Cost Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material Alpha | 500 kg | Regularly used across main lines. 300 kg in stock (historic cost 12/kg; scrap 8/kg); current replacement price **16/kg**. |
| Material Beta | 200 kg | Obsolete stock bought 2 years ago at 25/kg (book value 5,000). No internal use; would otherwise be scrapped immediately for **7/kg**. |
| Unskilled assembly | 300 hours | Permanent salaried staff (18/hr) who currently have **400 hours of idle spare capacity** this month. |
| Skilled welding | 150 hours | Paid **28/hr**, operating at **100% capacity** on Component Z (no overtime/hiring possible). Each hour diverted sacrifices **20/hr** of contribution (after already deducting the 28/hr wage). |
| Feasibility study | Completed | 3,500 paid last month. |
| Ultrasonic test rig | Dedicated hire | **2,400** incremental hire exclusively for this contract. |
| General factory fixed overhead | Absorbed | 4,000 allocated at normal absorption rate. |

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** For a material in continuous regular use by the business, the relevant cost of drawing units from inventory is their current replacement cost.
   - **b.** Past R&D/feasibility costs become relevant if the contract successfully goes ahead and recovers them.
   - **c.** Relevant cost-based minimum pricing defines a short-run floor for one-off spare/constrained decisions, whereas long-run survival requires covering full costs.
2. Calculate the relevant cost of each resource: (i) Material Alpha *(5 points)*, (ii) Material Beta *(5 points)*, (iii) Unskilled labour *(4 points)*, and (iv) Skilled welding *(5 points)*. *(19 points in total)*
3. Calculate: (i) The minimum relevant price (break-even cash floor) for the contract *(6 points)*, and (ii) The incremental profit gain from accepting at 23,500 *(4 points)*. *(10 points in total)*

1b. Sunk feasibility costs become relevant if the project proceeds
1c. Relevant pricing sets short-run floor; long-run requires full cost recovery

wiseflowFields.label: Incremental Profit Gain from Accepting at £23,500

hints: Material Alpha is in regular use, so drawing 300 kg from stock triggers 300 kg of replenishment + 200 kg bought fresh = all 500 kg @ £16 replacement cost. Material Beta is obsolete, so only its £7/kg forgone scrap matters.
Idle salaried staff cost £0 extra. Diverted welders cost £28/hr wage + £20/hr lost contribution = £48/hr. Ignore the £3,500 sunk study and £4,000 general fixed overhead.
rubricChecks: Valued Alpha at £16/kg replacement (£8,000) and Beta at £7/kg forgone NRV (£1,400)
Set idle salaried labour to £0 and scarce skilled labour to £48/hr (£7,200)
Excluded sunk feasibility (£3,500) and general overhead (£4,000) to find £19,000 floor & +£4,500 gain
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFB-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(sunk costs are past and irreversible regardless of project acceptance)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Relevant Cost Schedule:**
   - **Material Alpha (regularly used):** $500\text{ kg} \times £16 = \mathbf{£8,000}$.
   - **Material Beta (no other use):** Forgone scrap $= 200\text{ kg} \times £7 = \mathbf{£1,400}$ *(£25/kg historic cost is sunk)*.
   - **Unskilled labour:** Paid fixed salary with 400 idle hours $\implies \mathbf{£0}$.
   - **Skilled welding:** Direct wage $£28 +$ forgone Z contribution $£20 = £48/\text{hr} \times 150\text{ hrs} = \mathbf{£7,200}$.
   - **Rig hire:** **£2,400** *(£3,500 feasibility is sunk; £4,000 general overhead is non-incremental)*.
3. **Minimum Price & Gain:** $\text{Floor} = 8,000 + 1,400 + 0 + 7,200 + 2,400 = \mathbf{£19,000}$. Accepting £23,500 adds $23,500 - 19,000 = \mathbf{+£4,500}$ to profit.
questions.pitfall: Pricing the 300 kg of Alpha in stock at £12 historic cost instead of £16 replacement cost, or omitting the £20/hr lost contribution on scarce welders.

questions.title: WFB-E3 · Scandia Precision · Traditional DLH Overhead vs ABC & Mark-Up Pricing (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Scandia Precision AS** manufactures two products — **Standard** (`4,000` units) and **Custom** (`500` units). Direct cost and budgeted activity data are presented below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Metric | Standard (4,000 u) | Custom (500 u) | Factory Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Direct materials + direct labour per unit | 30.00 | 80.00 | — |
| Direct labour hours (DLH) per unit | 0.5 DLH | 2.0 DLH | **3,000 DLH** |
| Batch machine set-ups (total) | 50 set-ups | 100 set-ups | **150 set-ups** |
| Machine hours (MH, total) | 2,800 MH | 1,200 MH | **4,000 MH** |

**Budgeted indirect overheads (total 150,000):**

| Cost Pool | Budgeted Cost | Cost Driver |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Machine set-up pool | 90,000 | Number of set-ups |
| Machining pool | 60,000 | Machine hours (MH) |
| **Total indirect overheads** | **150,000** | |

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Activity-Based Costing is generally cheaper and simpler to administer than a single plant-wide DLH rate, so every small single-product business should adopt ABC.
   - **b.** Under a 25% mark-up on full cost (`Price = 1.25 × Full Cost`), under-costing Custom batches causes management to quote prices that fail to achieve the target profit margin.
   - **c.** Non-manufacturing period costs (e.g. corporate PR) are excluded from inventory valuation under IAS 2, though managers may consider all costs when setting long-run prices.
2. **Traditional costing (single plant-wide DLH rate):** Calculate: (i) Plant-wide overhead absorption rate per DLH *(4 points)*, and (ii) Traditional full cost per unit for Custom *(4 points)*. *(8 points in total)*
3. **Activity-Based Costing (ABC) & Pricing:** Calculate: (i) ABC cost driver rate per set-up *(3 points)*, (ii) ABC full cost per unit for Standard *(4 points)*, (iii) ABC full cost per unit for Custom *(5 points)*, and (iv) ABC selling price for Custom using a 25% cost-plus mark-up *(4 points)*. *(16 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. ABC is always cheaper to run and optimal for single-product firms
1b. Under-costing complex batches erodes realized margin under cost-plus pricing
1c. IAS 2 excludes non-production overheads from inventory valuation
Plant-Wide Overhead Rate per DLH
Traditional Full Cost per Unit — Custom
ABC Cost Driver Rate per Set-Up
ABC Full Cost per Unit — Standard
ABC Full Cost per Unit — Custom
ABC Selling Price for Custom at 25% Cost-Plus Mark-Up

hints: Traditional OAR = £150,000 / 3,000 DLH = £50/DLH; Custom uses 2.0 DLH/u so Traditional Full Cost = £80 + 2(£50) = £180.
ABC driver rates: £90,000 / 150 = £600/set-up and £60,000 / 4,000 = £15/MH. Allocate total pool pounds to Custom (500 units) first, divide by 500, add £80 direct cost, then multiply by 1.25!
rubricChecks: Computed Traditional OAR (£50/DLH) and Custom cost (£180/u)
Computed ABC full costs: Standard drops to £48/u while Custom rises to £236/u
Applied 25% mark-up on cost (236 × 1.25 = £295.00)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFB-E3 (30 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Wrong** *(ABC requires costly driver measurement and adds zero accuracy in a single-product firm)* · **1b. Right** · **1c. Right**.
2. **Traditional Costing:** $\text{OAR} = 150,000 / 3,000 = \mathbf{£50/\text{DLH}}$. Custom full cost $= 80 + 2.0(50) = \mathbf{£180.00/\text{u}}$ *(Standard $= 30 + 0.5(50) = £55.00/\text{u}$)*.
3. **ABC & Pricing:**
   - Rates: Set-ups $= 90,000 / 150 = \mathbf{£600/\text{set-up}}$ · Machining $= 60,000 / 4,000 = \mathbf{£15/\text{MH}}$.
   - **Standard (`4,000 u`):** Overhead $= 50(600) + 2,800(15) = 30,000 + 42,000 = £72,000$ (£18/u) $\implies$ Full cost $= 30 + 18 = \mathbf{£48.00/\text{u}}$.
   - **Custom (`500 u`):** Overhead $= 100(600) + 1,200(15) = 60,000 + 18,000 = £78,000$ (£156/u) $\implies$ Full cost $= 80 + 156 = \mathbf{£236.00/\text{u}}$.
   - **Custom 25% Mark-Up Price:** $236.00 \times 1.25 = \mathbf{£295.00/\text{u}}$.
questions.pitfall: Confusing 25% mark-up on cost (× 1.25) with a 25% margin on sales (÷ 0.75), or forgetting to divide Custom's £78,000 overhead pool by 500 units.

questions.title: WFB-E4 · Lücke Analytics · Lagged Receivables NPV & Residual Income Equivalence (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Lücke Analytics Ltd** considers a 3-year investment project at a cost of capital of **r = 10%**. Project cash flow and accrual specifications are summarized below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Specification | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Machine outlay (t = 0) | 90,000 |
| Expected salvage value in cash (t = 3) | 15,000 |

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Under clean-surplus accounting, the present value of all future Residual Incomes discounted at r equals the project's Net Present Value (NPV).
   - **b.** Even when total PV of Residual Income equals positive NPV, Year 1 Residual Income alone can be negative on back-loaded projects, tempting short-termist managers to reject positive-NPV investments.
   - **c.** Because NPV at 10% is positive here, the project's Internal Rate of Return (IRR) must be strictly lower than 10%.
