questions.title: WFC-E1 · Trondheim BioLabs · Equity Roll-Forward & Full Cash-Flow Reconciliation (40 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Trondheim BioLabs AS** has extracted the following balances and transaction data for the financial year ended **31 December 2026** (all figures in **£000**; use a minus sign `-` for net outflows):

| Balance Sheet Item (£000) | 1 Jan 2026 | 31 Dec 2026 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Total equity | 400 | 515 |
| Inventories | 50 | 44 |
| Trade receivables | 60 | 75 |
| Trade payables | 35 | 42 |
| Cash at bank | 14 | ? |

**Additional 2026 transactions (£000):**

- **a)** Issued new shares for **50** cash and paid cash dividends of **25** (classified under **Financing activities**). No revaluations occurred.
- **b)** Income statement includes loan interest expense of **12** (paid in cash) and tax expense of **18** (actual cash tax paid during 2026 was **20**).
- **c)** Operating profit (EBIT) is stated after charging depreciation of **32** and crediting a **gain on disposal** of lab equipment of **6** (the equipment was sold for **16** cash).
- **d)** Cash paid to purchase new lab equipment was **85**, and bank loan principal repaid was **30**.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** An accounting gain on disposal of equipment must be deducted from operating profit in the indirect cash-flow reconciliation so it is not double-counted alongside investing sale proceeds.
   - **b.** Repaying principal on a bank loan reduces Net Profit on the income statement.
   - **c.** If Opening Equity + New Shares + Net Profit − Dividends = Closing Equity, Net Profit can be deduced directly from SFP equity movements.
2. Deduce from the equity roll-forward and income items: (i) 2026 Net profit *(5 points)*, and (ii) 2026 Operating profit (EBIT) *(5 points)*. *(10 points in total)*
3. Prepare the Statement of Cash Flows figures (£000): (i) Cash generated from operations *(6 points)*, (ii) Net cash from operating activities *(5 points)*, (iii) Net cash from investing activities *(4 points)*, (iv) Net cash from financing activities *(4 points)*, and (v) Closing cash balance at 31 Dec 2026 *(5 points)*. *(24 points in total)*

1b. Loan principal repayment is an income statement expense

hints: First solve Equity roll-forward: 400 + 50 + Net Profit − 25 = 515 ⇒ Net Profit = 90. Add back interest (12) and tax charge (18) to reach EBIT = 120.
Cash generated = 120 + 32 (depr) − 6 (disposal gain!) + 6 (inv decrease) − 15 (AR increase) + 7 (AP increase) = 144. Deduct cash interest (12) and cash tax paid (20), NOT tax expense (18)!

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E1 (40 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(only interest is an expense; principal repayment reduces Cash and Loan Liability)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Profit Deduction (£000):** $400 + 50 + \text{NP} - 25 = 515 \implies \text{NP} = \mathbf{90}$. $\text{EBIT} = 90 + 12 + 18 = \mathbf{120}$.
3. **Cash Flows (£000):**
   - $\text{Cash generated} = 120 + 32 - 6 + (50 - 44) - (75 - 60) + (42 - 35) = 146 + 6 - 15 + 7 = \mathbf{144}$.
   - $\text{Net operating cash} = 144 - 12 - 20 = \mathbf{112}$.
   - $\text{Net investing cash} = -85 + 16 = \mathbf{-69}$.
   - $\text{Net financing cash} = +50 - 30 - 25 = \mathbf{-5}$.
   - $\text{Closing cash} = 14 + (112 - 69 - 5) = 14 + 38 = \mathbf{52}$.

questions.title: WFC-E2 · Aurora Ski Gear · Multi-Product Break-Even, Segment Continuation & Gearing (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Aurora Ski Gear AS** sells two product lines — **Alpine** (60% of unit mix) and **Nordic** (40% of unit mix) — at a current total volume of **4,000 units** (all currency figures in GBP):

| Product Line | Current Units | Selling Price / u | Variable Cost / u | Avoidable Line Fixed Cost | Apportioned HQ Fixed Cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Alpine (60%) | 2,400 | 300 | 180 | 70,000 | 50,000 |
| Nordic (40%) | 1,600 | 200 | 130 | 80,000 | 50,000 |
| **Company Total** | **4,000** | — | — | **150,000** | **100,000** |

Total company fixed costs are **250,000**. At 1,600 units, Nordic shows an accounting loss of `112,000 − 80,000 − 50,000 = −18,000`. Management is considering **dropping Nordic** (assuming **zero** HQ fixed cost savings and no impact on Alpine sales).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Multi-product break-even analysis assumes a constant sales mix; shifting the mix toward the higher-contribution product lowers the total break-even unit volume.
   - **b.** Because Nordic reports a −18,000 bottom-line loss after HQ apportionment, dropping Nordic will raise total company profit by +18,000.
   - **c.** Degree of operating gearing (`Total Contribution / Operating Profit`) predicts the percentage change in operating profit from a 1% change in volume (at constant mix).
2. **Multi-product break-even (60/40 mix):** Calculate: (i) Weighted-average contribution per unit *(5 points)*, (ii) Company break-even total units *(5 points)*, and (iii) Alpine units included inside the break-even mix *(5 points)*. *(15 points in total)*
3. **Keep-or-drop & Operating gearing:** Calculate: (i) Current total company operating profit at 4,000 units *(4 points)*, (ii) Change in company profit if Nordic is dropped (use minus sign if profit falls) *(6 points)*, and (iii) Degree of operating gearing to 2 decimals *(4 points)*. *(14 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Shifting sales mix toward higher-CM product lowers break-even units
1b. Dropping Nordic increases company profit by +£18,000
1c. Operating gearing ratio measures profit elasticity to volume
Weighted-Average Contribution per Unit (£)
Company Break-Even Total Units (Alpine + Nordic combined)
Alpine Units Included inside Company Break-Even Mix
Current Total Company Operating Profit (at 4,000 units)
Change in Company Profit if Nordic is Dropped (use minus sign!)
Degree of Operating Gearing (Contribution / Profit, 2 decimals)

hints: Unit CMs: Alpine = £120, Nordic = £70. Weighted CM = 0.60(120) + 0.40(70) = £100/u. Divide total £250,000 fixed costs by £100/u, then take 60% for Alpine.
Nordic earns £112,000 contribution and saves only £80,000 avoidable fixed cost if closed — losing +£32,000 net contribution toward HQ! Use a minus sign (−32000).
rubricChecks: Calculated weighted CM (£100/u), total BEP (2,500 units), and Alpine BEP share (1,500 units)
Identified −£32,000 profit drop from closing Nordic (ignoring unavoidable £50k HQ overhead)
Computed company profit (£150,000) and operating gearing (400,000 / 150,000 = 2.67)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(company profit falls by £32,000)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Multi-Product Break-Even:**
   - $\text{Weighted CM} = 0.6(120) + 0.4(70) = \mathbf{£100/\text{unit}}$.
   - $\text{Total BEP} = 250,000 / 100 = \mathbf{2,500\text{ units}}$ (`60% × 2,500 =` **1,500 Alpine** + `1,000 Nordic`).
3. **Keep-or-Drop & Operating Gearing:**
   - Current Contribution $= 4,000 \times 100 = £400,000 \implies \text{Operating Profit} = 400,000 - 250,000 = \mathbf{£150,000}$.
   - Dropping Nordic loses $£112,000$ contribution while saving only $£80,000$ avoidable fixed cost $\implies \Delta\text{Profit} = \mathbf{-£32,000}$ *(new profit $= £118,000$)*.
   - $\text{Operating Gearing} = 400,000 / 150,000 = \mathbf{2.67}$.
questions.pitfall: Entering +32000 instead of -32000 for the profit impact of dropping Nordic, or dividing £150k avoidable FC instead of £250k total FC for company break-even.

questions.title: WFC-E3 · Krono Manufacturing · Service Dept Re-Apportionment & Margin Pricing (25 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
The following factory overhead budget has been extracted for **Krono Manufacturing AS** (all currency figures in GBP):

| Department | Type | Direct Dept. Overhead | Machine Hours (MH) | Direct Labour Hours (DLH) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Machining | Production | 140,000 | 7,000 | 1,000 |
| Assembly | Production | 82,000 | 500 | 5,000 |
| Maintenance | Service | 60,000 | — | — |
| **Total** | | **282,000** | **7,500** | **6,000** |

Maintenance department costs are re-apportioned **70% to Machining** and **30% to Assembly** before calculating departmental absorption rates (Machining absorbs on **MH**; Assembly absorbs on **DLH**).

**For specific customer order "Job 405", the following is required:**
- Direct materials: **4,200**
- Direct labour: **2,800**
- Machining time: **80 MH** · Assembly time: **60 DLH**
- Krono quotes selling prices to achieve a **20% profit margin on selling price** (`Price = Full Cost / 0.80`).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Service department costs (such as factory maintenance) are re-apportioned to production cost centres so product units passing through production absorb them.
   - **b.** Because Machining has 7,000 MH vs 1,000 DLH, direct labour hours is a better absorption basis than machine hours for Machining.
   - **c.** A 20% profit margin on selling price is mathematically equivalent to a 25% mark-up on full cost.
2. Calculate the departmental overhead absorption rates after re-apportioning Maintenance: (i) Machining overhead rate per MH *(4 points)*, and (ii) Assembly overhead rate per DLH *(4 points)*. *(8 points in total)*
3. For **Job 405**, calculate: (i) Total overhead absorbed *(3 points)*, (ii) Full cost *(4 points)*, and (iii) Quoted selling price for a 20% margin on sales *(4 points)*. *(11 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Service centre overheads are re-apportioned to production centres
1b. DLH is superior to MH in capital-intensive Machining
1c. 20% margin on sales equals 25% mark-up on cost
Machining Overhead Rate per MH (after 70% Maintenance share)
Assembly Overhead Rate per DLH (after 30% Maintenance share)
Total Overhead Absorbed by Job 405
Full Cost of Job 405
Quoted Selling Price for 20% Margin on Sales

hints: Job 405 Full Cost = £4,200 + £2,800 + 80(£26) + 60(£20) = £10,280. For a 20% margin on selling price, divide £10,280 by 0.80!
rubricChecks: Re-apportioned £60,000 Maintenance (70/30) to obtain £26/MH and £20/DLH
Calculated Job 405 overhead (£3,280) and Full Cost (£10,280)
Divided Full Cost by 0.80 for 20% sales margin (£12,850.00)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E3 (25 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(Machining is machine-paced, so MH is the cause-and-effect driver)* · **1c. Right** ($0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25 = 25\%$).
2. **Departmental Rates & Job 405:**
   - **Machining:** $(140,000 + 42,000) / 7,000\text{ MH} = 182,000 / 7,000 = \mathbf{£26.00/\text{MH}}$.
   - **Assembly:** $(82,000 + 18,000) / 5,000\text{ DLH} = 100,000 / 5,000 = \mathbf{£20.00/\text{DLH}}$.
   - **Job 405 Overhead:** $80(26) + 60(20) = 2,080 + 1,200 = \mathbf{£3,280}$.
   - **Job 405 Full Cost:** $4,200 + 2,800 + 3,280 = \mathbf{£10,280}$.
   - **Selling Price (20% margin on price):** $10,280 / (1 - 0.20) = \mathbf{£12,850.00}$.
questions.pitfall: Multiplying £10,280 by 1.20 (£12,336) instead of dividing by 0.80 (£12,850) when pricing for a 20% margin on sales.

questions.title: WFC-E4 · Solberg Energy · Mutually Exclusive NPV, IRR Interpolation & Scale Conflict (40 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Solberg Energy AS** is choosing between two **mutually exclusive** 3-year projects at a cost of capital of **r = 12%** (no capital rationing; all currency figures in GBP):

| Year | Project Alpha | Project Beta |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| t = 0 (Initial outlay) | −100,000 | −200,000 |
| t = 1 | +70,000 | +100,000 |
| t = 2 | +60,000 | +100,000 |
| t = 3 | +20,000 | +100,000 |

*(12% discount factors: t = 1: `0.8929`, t = 2: `0.7972`, t = 3: `0.7118`; 3-year 12% annuity factor = `2.4018`. At a 30% test rate, Project Alpha's exact NPV is `−1,547.56`.)*

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** A project with non-conventional cash flows (multiple sign changes) can exhibit more than one mathematical IRR or no real IRR.
   - **b.** Payback period penalises projects whose largest cash inflows arrive after the payback cut-off date.
   - **c.** When two mutually exclusive projects have positive NPVs, a wealth-maximising firm should always pick the project with the shorter payback period.
2. Calculate: (i) Payback period for Project Alpha *(4 points)*, (ii) Payback period for Project Beta *(4 points)*, (iii) NPV of Project Alpha at 12% *(5 points)*, and (iv) NPV of Project Beta at 12% *(5 points)*. *(18 points in total)*
3. Calculate: (i) Interpolated IRR of Project Alpha between 12% and 30% *(6 points)*, (ii) Extra NPV wealth created by Beta over Alpha *(5 points)*, and (iii) State which mutually exclusive project Solberg should accept *(5 points)*. *(16 points in total)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Non-conventional cash flows can yield multiple IRRs
1b. Payback ignores cash inflows after the payback point
1c. Shortest payback always maximises shareholder wealth

wiseflowFields.group: 2. Payback & Net Present Values at 12% (18 pts)
wiseflowFields.label: NPV of Project Alpha at 12%

wiseflowFields.label: NPV of Project Beta at 12%
Interpolated IRR of Project Alpha between 12% and 30% (enter % e.g. 27.86)
Extra NPV Wealth Created by Beta over Alpha (£)
Which mutually exclusive project should Solberg accept?

hints: Alpha recovers £70k in Year 1 and needs £30k out of £60k in Year 2 ⇒ 1.50 years. For Beta, multiply £100,000 by the 3-year 12% annuity factor (2.40183) and subtract £200,000.
Interpolate Alpha's IRR between 12% (+£24,565.87) and 30% (−£1,593.08): 12% + [24,565.87 / (24,565.87 + 1,593.08)] × 18%. Compare absolute NPVs at 12% for the mutually exclusive decision!
rubricChecks: Calculated Paybacks (Alpha 1.50 yrs, Beta 2.00 yrs) and NPVs at 12% (+£24,566 vs +£40,183)
Interpolated Alpha's IRR (~28.9% linear / 27.8% exact)
Selected Project Beta on higher NPV (+£15,617 extra shareholder wealth) despite Alpha's higher IRR
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E4 (40 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Right** · **1c. Wrong** *(maximise NPV, not payback speed)*.
2. **Payback & NPV (12%):**
   - **Payback:** Alpha $= 1 + 30,000/60,000 = \mathbf{1.50\text{ yrs}}$ · Beta $= 200,000/100,000 = \mathbf{2.00\text{ yrs}}$.
   - **NPV Alpha:** $-100,000 + 70,000/1.12 + 60,000/1.12^2 + 20,000/1.12^3 = \mathbf{+£24,567.24}$ *(3-dec factors: +£24,570.00)*.
   - **NPV Beta:** $-200,000 + 100,000 \times 2.401831 = \mathbf{+£40,183.13}$ *(3-dec annuity 2.402: +£40,200.00)*.
3. **IRR Interpolation & Selection:**
   - $\text{IRR}_{\text{Alpha}} \approx 12\% + \frac{24,567.24}{24,567.24 - (-1,547.56)} \times (30\% - 12\%) = \mathbf{28.93\%}$ *(exact IRR $= 27.79\%$, within ±2%/alt tolerance)*.
   - **Decision:** Accept **Project Beta** — although Alpha has faster payback (1.50 yrs) and higher IRR (~28% vs Beta's ~23.4%), Beta is twice the scale and creates **+£15,615.89** more net present value for shareholders.
questions.pitfall: Picking Alpha for its higher IRR/faster payback when Beta delivers £15,617 more NPV wealth.

questions.title: Exercise 1: Measuring and reporting financial position
questions.promptMarkdown:
Nora started a new design business on **01. May**. To do so, she opened a business bank account and transferred **60,000** of her own money into it. During the first month of operations, the following additional transactions took place:

- **a)** She borrowed **40,000** from Oslo Commercial Bank and paid the money into the business bank account.
- **b)** She paid **48,000** cash for a small studio unit (premises).
- **c)** She paid **5,000** cash for a second-hand delivery van.
- **d)** She bought goods for resale (inventories) for **12,000**, paying immediately, and bought further goods for **24,000** on credit.
- **e)** She sold goods which had cost **18,000** for **32,000**. Of this revenue, **8,000** was received in cash and the remaining **24,000** was on credit.
- **f)** She paid **300** cash for fuel for the van, all of which was used during May.
- **g)** She received **9,000** cash from trade receivables.
- **h)** She paid **400** cash to Oslo Commercial Bank as interest on the loan for May.

Ignore depreciation of non-current assets.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** The Statement of Financial Position sets out the assets of a business and the claims (equity and liabilities) against those assets at a specific point in time.
   - **b.** Inventories held for resale are classified as non-current assets because they are physical goods.
   - **c.** Under the dual aspect convention, every transaction affects at least two items so the accounting equation always remains in balance.
2. Open a beginning-of-May Statement of Financial Position for Nora's business (total assets and opening equity). *(6 points)*
3. Track transactions **a)** to **h)** as pluses and minuses to determine every end-of-May Statement of Financial Position balance (Cash, Trade receivables, Inventories, Trade payables, Borrowings). *(24 points)*
4. State the end-of-May **Total Assets** and **Closing Equity** on Nora's Statement of Financial Position. *(10 points)*
5. Calculate the **profit** Nora's business earned in May. *(4 points)*
hints: Start with Opening Cash = 60,000 and Opening Equity = 60,000, then adjust every cash inflow/outflow across a)–h).
Only transactions e) (+14,000 gross profit), f) (−300 fuel), and h) (−400 interest) affect profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (inventories are current assets), `1c = Right`.

**2. Beginning-of-May SFP (6 pts):** Cash = `60,000` · Total Assets = `60,000` · Opening Equity = `60,000`.

**3. End-of-May balances (24 pts):**
- **Cash:** `60,000 + 40,000 − 48,000 − 5,000 − 12,000 + 8,000 − 300 + 9,000 − 400 = 51,300`
- **Trade receivables:** `24,000 − 9,000 = 15,000`
- **Inventories:** `12,000 + 24,000 − 18,000 = 18,000`
- **Trade payables:** `24,000` · **Borrowings:** `40,000`

**4. End-of-May SFP totals (10 pts):**
- Non-current assets: Premises `48,000` + Van `5,000` = `53,000`
- Current assets: Inventories `18,000` + Receivables `15,000` + Cash `51,300` = `84,300`
- **Total Assets:** `53,000 + 84,300 = 137,300`
- **Closing Equity:** `60,000 + 13,300 = 73,300` (`Equity 73,300 + Borrowings 40,000 + Payables 24,000 = 137,300 ✓`)

**5. May Profit (4 pts):** `(32,000 − 18,000) − 300 − 400 = 13,300` (transactions **e**, **f**, and **h** affect profit).
questions.pitfall: Receiving 9,000 from receivables (g) and borrowing 40,000 (a) change Cash, NOT profit!

questions.title: Exercise 2: Break-even analysis
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Lillehammer Services AS** provides a single standard service. The business's results for a representative month are as follows:

| Metric | Monthly Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Sales [units of service] | 800 |
| Sales revenue | 48,000 |
| Operating profit | 18,000 |

There were no changes in selling price or cost structure over the period. Variable costs were **15** per unit of service.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Contribution per unit equals selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit.
   - **b.** Irrelevant costs include future differential cash flows.
   - **c.** At the break-even point, total contribution equals total fixed costs and operating profit is zero.
2. Calculate the **selling price per unit** and the **fixed costs per month**. *(6 points)*
3. Calculate the **break-even point** in units and in sales revenue. *(6 points)*
4. Calculate: (i) the **margin of safety (%)** at 800 units *(6 points)*, and (ii) the monthly **units required** to earn a target operating profit of **27,000** *(6 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
hints: Selling price = Sales revenue ÷ Units; Fixed costs = Total Contribution − Operating Profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (future differential cash flows are relevant), `1c = Right`.

**2. Price & Fixed Costs (6 pts):**
- Selling price = `48,000 / 800 = 60` per unit
- Contribution per unit = `60 − 15 = 45`
- Total contribution = `800 × 45 = 36,000` ⇒ Fixed costs = `36,000 − 18,000 = 18,000`

**3. Break-even point (6 pts):**
- Break-even units = `18,000 / 45 = 400` units
- Break-even revenue = `400 × 60 = 24,000`

**4. Margin of Safety & Target Profit (12 pts):**
- Margin of safety (%) = `(800 − 400) / 800 × 100% = 50%`
- Target units for 27,000 profit = `(18,000 + 27,000) / 45 = 1,000` units
questions.pitfall: Never subtract total cost per unit instead of variable cost per unit when computing contribution!

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Contribution/unit = Price − Variable cost/unit
1b. Irrelevant costs include future differential cash flows
1c. At break-even, total contribution equals fixed costs

questions.title: Exercise 3: Full costing
questions.promptMarkdown:
The following information has been taken from the budget for the forthcoming financial year of **Drammen Metalworks AS**:

| Budgeted Activity / Manufacturing Cost | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Direct labor hours [hours] | 80,000 |
| Machine hours [hours] | 60,000 |
| Direct labor | 480,000 |
| Indirect labor | 96,000 |
| Direct materials | 160,000 |
| Power | 32,000 |
| Factory heat and light | 8,000 |
| Machine maintenance | 40,000 |
| Cleaning material | 4,000 |
| Depreciation: factory | 100,000 |
| Depreciation: machinery | 280,000 |
| **Total manufacturing costs** | **1,200,000** |

All direct labor is paid at the same hourly rate.

For the specific order **"No 204"**, the following is required:
- Direct materials: **6,500**
- Direct labor hours: **3,000 [hours]**
- Machine hours: **1,400 [hours]**

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Indirect costs are costs that cannot be directly measured in respect of a particular job or cost unit.
   - **b.** Direct labor and direct materials should be included in the overhead pool when calculating the overhead recovery rate.
   - **c.** Full cost information is used for inventory valuation and long-run pricing decisions.
2. Calculate the **overhead recovery rate** based on direct labor hours. *(4 points)*
3. Calculate the **direct labor cost**, **overheads absorbed**, and **full cost** for order **"No 204"** using the overhead rate based on direct labor hours. *(10 points)*
hints: Total overheads = Total manufacturing costs (1,200,000) minus Direct labor (480,000) and Direct materials (160,000).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (direct costs are traced directly, never put into the overhead pool), `1c = Right`.

**2. Overhead recovery rate (4 pts):**
- Total indirect overheads = `1,200,000 − 480,000 − 160,000 = 560,000`
- Overhead recovery rate = `560,000 / 80,000 DLH = 7.00` per DLH

**3. Full cost for order "No 204" (10 pts):**
- Direct labor hourly rate = `480,000 / 80,000 = 6.00` per DLH
- Direct materials = `6,500`
- Direct labor = `3,000 × 6.00 = 18,000`
- Overheads absorbed = `3,000 × 7.00 = 21,000`
- **Full cost of order "No 204"** = `6,500 + 18,000 + 21,000 = 45,500`
questions.pitfall: Do NOT include Direct Labor or Direct Materials in the numerator of the overhead recovery rate — subtract both from 1,200,000 first!

1b. Include direct labor & materials in overhead pool
1c. Full costing supports inventory valuation & pricing

questions.title: Exercise 4: Net present value
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Solheim Industri AS** considers implementing an investment project with a useful life of **three years**. To implement the project, Solheim needs to buy a machine in **t = 0** for **60,000**. At the end of the three years in **t = 3**, the machine can be sold for **12,000**.

The machine produces **1,200 units** of a product each year from **t = 1** until **t = 3** at variable cash costs of **12 per unit** (paid immediately). The sales pattern is as follows:

| Period | Price per Unit | Sales Quantity | Cash Collection Pattern |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| t = 1 | 34 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for 600 units; payment for 600 units in t = 2 |
| t = 2 | 30 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for 600 units; payment for 600 units in t = 3 |
| t = 3 | 30 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for all 1,200 units |

The cost of capital is **r = 0.1** (10%; discount factor for t = 3 is `0.7513`; the other discount factors need to be calculated).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** The accounting rate of return (ARR) is the average accounting profit from the project expressed as a percentage of the average investment.
   - **b.** Payback period (PP) is the length of time until an initial investment generates cumulative operating profit equal to its cost.
   - **c.** Net present value (NPV) is the sum of the discounted values of all net cash flows from an investment.
2. Calculate the net cash flows for t = 1, t = 2, t = 3 and the **Net Present Value (NPV)** at 10%. *(14 points)*
3. Calculate the **net income** from the project for each period **t = 1**, **t = 2**, and **t = 3**. Assume straight-line depreciation of the machine. *(14 points)*
4. What is the **total present value (in t = 0)** of the periods' **residual income**? *(No extra calculation necessary.)* *(2 points)*
5. Is the **internal rate of return (IRR)** larger or smaller than **10%**? *(4 points)*
hints: Annual straight-line depreciation = (60,000 − 12,000) / 3 = 16,000; Preinreich–Lücke theorem guarantees PV(Residual Income) = NPV.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (payback measures **cash flows**, not operating profit), `1c = Right`.

**2. Cash Flows & NPV at 10% (14 pts):**
- Variable cash outflow each year = `1,200 × 12 = 14,400`
- `CF₀ = −60,000`
- `CF₁ = (600 × 34) − 14,400 = 20,400 − 14,400 = 6,000`
- `CF₂ = (600 × 34) + (600 × 30) − 14,400 = 38,400 − 14,400 = 24,000`
- `CF₃ = (600 × 30) + (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 + 12,000 = 51,600`
- `NPV = −60,000 + 6,000/1.1 + 24,000/1.1² + 51,600/1.1³ = −60,000 + 5,454.55 + 19,834.71 + 38,767.84 = 4057.1`

**3. Accrual Net Income t = 1..3 (14 pts):**
- Straight-line depreciation = `(60,000 − 12,000) / 3 = 16,000` per year
- `NI₁ = (1,200 × 34) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 10,400`
- `NI₂ = (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 5,600`
- `NI₃ = (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 5,600`

**4. Total PV of Residual Income at t = 0 (2 pts):** By the Preinreich–Lücke theorem, `PV(RI) = NPV = 4057.1` (no extra calculation needed!).

**5. IRR vs 10% (4 pts):** Because `NPV > 0` at `10%` on a conventional investment, the IRR must be **Larger than 10%**.
questions.pitfall: Remember that Net Income uses invoiced accrual sales (1,200 units/yr) minus depreciation, whereas NPV uses cash collections and ignores depreciation!

1b. Payback period measures operating profit recovery

questions.title: T7.1 · Session 7 · Speedy Delivery Ltd (Payback, NPV & Residual Income)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Speedy Delivery Ltd** is considering investing in a fleet of new delivery trucks to expand its delivery services. The trucks cost **£500,000**, have a useful life of **5 years**, and an estimated salvage value of **£50,000** at the end of Year 5. They will be depreciated on a **straight-line** basis. The investment is expected to generate additional annual revenue of **£200,000** and incur annual operating expenses of **£50,000**.

| Parameter | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Initial cost of trucks ($I_0$) | £500,000 |
| Useful life | 5 years |
| Estimated salvage value ($t=5$) | £50,000 |
| Annual revenue | £200,000 |
| Annual operating expenses (cash) | £50,000 |
| Discount rate / required return ($r$) | 10% |

**Required:**
1. Calculate the **Payback Period** for the investment.
2. Calculate the **Net Present Value (NPV)** of the investment using a discount rate of $10\%$.
3. Calculate the **Residual Income (RI)** for each year ($t = 1, \dots, 5$), using a required return of $10\%$ and the opening carrying value of the trucks as operating assets ($OA_{t-1}$). **Show that the present value of the residual incomes equals the NPV.**
rubricChecks: Annual operating cash flow $C = £200,000 - £50,000 = £150,000$; Year 5 total inflow $= £150,000 + £50,000 = £200,000$
Payback Period $= £500,000 / £150,000 = \mathbf{3.33\text{ years}}$ (3 years 4 months)
Opening carrying values $OA_{t-1}$: £500k, £410k, £320k, £230k, £140k → $RI_t = £10\text{k}, £19\text{k}, £28\text{k}, £37\text{k}, £46\text{k}$
Total Present Value of Residual Income $TPV(RI) = £9,091 + £15,702 + £21,037 + £25,271 + £28,562 = \mathbf{£99,664 = NPV}$
hints: Hint 1: Separate **cash flows** (ignoring depreciation!) from **accounting profit** (which deducts straight-line depreciation of $(500,000 - 50,000)/5 = £90,000$/year).

Hint 2: For Residual Income, charge $10\%$ on the **opening** carrying value $OA_{t-1}$ at the start of each year: $OA_0 = £500,000$, $OA_1 = £410,000$, $OA_2 = £320,000$, $OA_3 = £230,000$, $OA_4 = £140,000$.
Hint 3: Discount each year's $RI_t = \text{Net Income}_t - 0.10 \cdot OA_{t-1}$ back to $t=0$ at $10\%$ — the Preinreich–Lücke theorem guarantees $\sum PV(RI_t) = \text{NPV}$.
questions.pitfall: Two classic traps: (1) deducting £90,000 depreciation from cash flows when computing Payback or NPV (depreciation is non-cash!), and (2) using **closing** carrying value $OA_t$ instead of **opening** carrying value $OA_{t-1}$ in $RI_t = NI_t - r \cdot OA_{t-1}$, which breaks the $TPV(RI) = NPV$ identity.

questions.title: T7.2 · Session 7 · Logistics Solutions Ltd (Uneven Cash Flows, Payback & NPV)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Logistics Solutions Ltd** is considering an investment in a new automated warehousing system to improve efficiency and reduce labour costs. The project requires an upfront capital investment of **£2,000,000** ($t=0$), has an estimated useful life of **7 years**, a residual (salvage) value of **£200,000** at the end of Year 7 (already included in the Year 7 total below), and a discount rate of **12%**.

| Year | Expected Cash Flow (£) |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | $(2,000,000)$ |
| 1 | 300,000 |
| 2 | 450,000 |
| 3 | 500,000 |
| 4 | 550,000 |
| 5 | 450,000 |
| 6 | 400,000 |
| 7 | $250,000 + 200,000\text{ (salvage)} = 450,000$ |

**Required:**
1. Calculate the **Payback Period** for the project.
2. Calculate the **Net Present Value (NPV)** of the project using a discount rate of $12\%$.
3. Based on the NPV and payback period, provide a **recommendation** on whether Logistics Solutions Ltd should proceed with the investment.
rubricChecks: Cumulative cash flows: Y1 $-£1,700\text{k}$, Y2 $-£1,250\text{k}$, Y3 $-£750\text{k}$, Y4 $-£200\text{k}$, Y5 $+£250\text{k}$
Payback Period $= 4 + \frac{200,000}{450,000} = \mathbf{4.44\text{ years}}$ (4 years, 5 months)
Discount each cash flow at $12\%$ (3-dp table factors: 0.893, 0.797, 0.712, 0.636, 0.567, 0.507, 0.452) → **NPV = −£6,300** (exact unrounded: **−£6,429**)

Recommendation: **Reject** on purely financial grounds (negative NPV fails to meet the 12% required return), unless unquantified strategic/non-financial benefits (e.g. customer satisfaction, labour stability) outweigh the slight value reduction
hints: Hint 1: Because cash flows are **uneven**, build a cumulative cash flow column starting at $-£2,000,000$ to locate the exact year where the sign flips from negative to positive (between Year 4 and Year 5).
Hint 2: Do NOT add £200,000 salvage value twice — the table already shows Year 7 $= 250,000 + 200,000 = £450,000$.

Hint 3: Remember that NPV is the **primary decision rule** (wealth maximisation): a slightly negative NPV means the project earns less than the 12% cost of capital, even if the 4.44-year payback looks reasonable.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
### 1. Payback Period (Uneven Cash Flows)

| Year | Cash Flow (£) | Cumulative Cash Flow (£) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | $(2,000,000)$ | $(2,000,000)$ |
| 1 | 300,000 | $(1,700,000)$ |
| 2 | 450,000 | $(1,250,000)$ |
| 3 | 500,000 | $(750,000)$ |
| 4 | 550,000 | $(200,000)$ |
| 5 | 450,000 | $+250,000$ |
| 6 | 400,000 | $+650,000$ |
| 7 | 450,000 | $+1,100,000$ |

At the end of Year 4, £200,000 remains unrecovered, and Year 5 generates £450,000:
$$\text{Payback Period} = 4 + \frac{200,000}{450,000} = 4 + 0.44 = \mathbf{4.44\text{ years}} \text{ (4 years, 5 months)}$$

### 2. Net Present Value (NPV at $r = 12\%$)
Using the standard 3-decimal BI Present Value table factors $(1.12)^{-t}$:

| Year $t$ | Cash Flow (£) | 12% Table Factor | Present Value (£) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | $(2,000,000)$ | 1.000 | $(2,000,000)$ |
| 1 | 300,000 | 0.893 | 267,900 |
| 2 | 450,000 | 0.797 | 358,650 |
| 3 | 500,000 | 0.712 | 356,000 |
| 4 | 550,000 | 0.636 | 349,800 |
| 5 | 450,000 | 0.567 | 255,150 |
| 6 | 400,000 | 0.507 | 202,800 |
| 7 | 450,000 | 0.452 | 203,400 |
| **Total** | **1,100,000** | | **NPV = −£6,300** |

*(Note: Using exact unrounded powers $1 / 1.12^t$ on a calculator gives **NPV = −£6,428.86**; both are accepted in WISEflow grading.)*

### 3. Investment Recommendation
- **Payback Period:** $4.44$ years (out of a 7-year useful life) may look acceptable depending on management's target cut-off.
- **NPV:** Negative (**−£6,300**), meaning the project earns slightly below the required $12\%$ hurdle rate and reduces shareholder wealth.
- **Conclusion:** **Do not proceed** on purely financial grounds. However, because the NPV is only marginally negative relative to a £2 million project, Logistics Solutions Ltd might still reconsider if significant **strategic or non-financial benefits** not captured in the cash flows (e.g., improved customer satisfaction, higher reliability, reduced labour turnover) clearly outweigh £6,300.
questions.pitfall: Double-counting the £200,000 salvage value in Year 7 (it is already summed into £450,000), or recommending acceptance simply because total undiscounted cash flows are positive (+£1.1M) and payback is under 5 years.
